utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon everybody, and good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, all the accused are present. Prosecution is represented only by -- today only by Mr. Thayer, I understand Mr. McCloskey won't be with us today and tomorrow but possibly on Friday. Amongst the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Josse and Mr. Haynes, am I right? And Mr. Petrusic is not here as well. Okay. Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And as presiding judge, I welcome you to this Tribunal. You've been summoned by the Nikolic Defence team as one of the witnesses. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth in the course of your evidence. Madam usher has already given you the text of the solemn declaration, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric, please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon will be putting some questions to you. He will then be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President. Good afternoon judges, good afternoon colleagues. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the record, allow me to introduce myself, my name is Stephane Bourgon, along with my colleagues Ms. Jelena Nikolic and Ms. Marie-Claude Fournie we represent Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. Before we begin I would like to remind you of two things. The first one is I would have quite a few questions to ask you today, and I want to make sure if you do not understand any of my questions that you do not hesitate to stop me so I can take that question over again. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the second thing is I would ask simply to cooperate with the interpreters and allow them to do their work, that you always wait until I finish my question before you provide me with any answer. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then we are ready to begin. Please state your name in full for the record?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Mico Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, and how old are you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of September 1957. I'm 51 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The village of Obradici, Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, before the war, what was your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was a mining technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you work in any specific place?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I worked in the zinc mine called Sase in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And today, sir, what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I am a private entrepreneur.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And which area do you work, area means what type of work is your business in?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I live in Bratunac where my company is. I do wood processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you have any employees in your company, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There are 35 permanently employed people, and 15 contractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you before the war have any service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you share with us where and what you did in the JNA before the war?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I completed the reserve officer's school. My specialty is ground artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how long were you at the -- you said the reserve officer's school, how long were you in that school?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And following this seven months, did you continue serving with the JNA, or was that it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of the course after seven months, I was first sent to the 3rd Guard's Regiment of the 1st army. I taught firing and targeting for seven months at the reserve officer's school in Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that you did mention this, but what year was this?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I began serving the term in 1978 and returned home on the 2nd of November 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I understand that during the war you were mobilised in the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also, I think this is not in dispute, that you were a member of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you do in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: From the 14th of November 1992 when the brigade was formed, I was appointed chief of artillery in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you continue in that same position until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what was your rank in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you wear actually rank insignias on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I frequently did, but on occasion I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you share with us what occasions or in which occasions you would not wear your rank?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If we were to be engaged in combat, especially during the night, it was then that I did not wear any insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, who was your commander in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, before I start to ask you some specific questions about the events which took place in the war, I'd like to ask you this: Is this the first time that you testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In what case or cases have you testified before?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The Colonel Blagojevic and Lieutenant Jokic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who called you to testify at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I believe the attorney's name was Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was that with the Prosecution or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a member of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And prior to your testimony in that case, did you have the opportunity to meet with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when was that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I believe it was on the 27th or the 28th of November 2001 in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you recall if this interview was recorded?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did the Prosecution ever indicate that they were interested in calling you as a witness?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was there in the capacity of a witness. I don't know what their future intentions may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe, sir, my question was not precise. Did the Prosecution ever indicate to you that they would like to call you as a witness in a trial?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you met with the Prosecution, do you remember what they were interested in from you, what information they wished to discuss with you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I met with the Prosecution, they were interested in the period of July 1995, and Srebrenica in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, in the end, did you ever testify for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not. It was cancelled at the last moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain us, did you take any steps or were you about to testify or when was it that this was cancelled?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was probably in February 2004 in the Major Obrenovic case. I was called. I handed over my passport and a visa was supposed to be issued. I was scheduled to fly in two day's time. However, at the last moment, around 3.50 in the afternoon, I received a phone call from the Prosecutor's Office, I presume. I was told that I no longer needed to appear and that Major Obrenovic had reached an agreement with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like now to move on and to focus on the days following the fall of Srebrenica in July of 1995. Sir, do you remember this period in general?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And shortly after the fall of Srebrenica, do you recall having to go to the Zvornik area for an assignment?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you remember what was -- on what date you went to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was between the 14th and the 15th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, how do you remember this date with so much precision?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: For the first time during my service, it happened that I had to refuse an order to my brigade commander. That was one thing. Another thing was that I was supposed to go to a certain area with my soldiers and on our way there, we would have been put in danger. I was supposed to go there with a unit that had been trained in artillery rather than in infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, can you share with us what happened when you received this assignment from, I believe you received it from your commander?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th around midnight, military police came. I was resting at my family home. They told me that I was supposed to go to the command on the brigade commander's orders, Colonel Blagojevic. I got ready quickly and arrived at the brigade command to the duty operation officer's room. I encountered Lieutenant-Colonel Blagojevic there as well as Major Dragan Trisic. He told me that he was ordered to send a unit to the area of Zvornik to the Zvornik Brigade for assistance. He decided that it was my unit that was to be sent. I flatly refused. I said that my unit was not intended for infantry combat. I also said that my unit had been trained to engage in combat by using artillery pieces alone. He did not show much understanding, but I wouldn't budge. It was a difficult conversation. At a certain point, Dragan Trisic moved away and then returned trying to exert some more pressure, and I said yes, I will go, but I want a written order. He said well, I can't and then I said, I can't go. It took a while and at a later point I said, I will go but I want to know when my replacement will come. He said, I guarantee that you will be replaced tomorrow before noon. He wanted to know why I was refusing to go, and I said, I can't go there with my unit at this hour, especially knowing that there were large enemy soldier groups breaking through along that axis and that there is always a good chance of us being attacked on our way there. That was one thing. Another thing, I was supposed to go to a unit the area of which I was not familiar with. I don't know who was to my left and to my right. There were also many other reasons due to which I refused to get into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the end, sir, did you finally accept the task from your commander, and did you get that written order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Not in writing. I did accept to go, following the brigade commander's explanation that he was to send the replacements by tomorrow 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did your commander inform you who he had received the order from to send a unit to the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, from a superior command. I presume the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, is it normal in the military to ask for a written order, as you did?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It is not customary, but I had good reasons and arguments on my side. There was this chance of us being ambushed along the way. I might survive it, but then I would have to go back to a community, to an environment alive, whereas the rest would have been dead. That was my reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, what steps did you take in order to execute or to perform this task?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I accepted the order, I called my unit commanders and ordered that a number of people should be left behind to secure firing positions. The rest of the soldiers were to pick up their equipment and personal weapons and show up in front of the brigade command in order to go on a mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened then, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In a very short time my officers brought the howitzer and 122-millimetre cannon crews, they were in front of the brigade command and a bus awaited us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What kind of bus was this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian bus for passenger traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What time was it when you boarded the bus to be on your way towards Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think around 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did your men keep their weapons with them while they were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. When we boarded the bus, I told them that they should have their weapons loaded because we can be easily ambushed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, sir, did anything particular happen on the way or on the road between Bratunac and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On our way from Bratunac towards Zvornik, some 2 kilometres from Bratunac, a part of our unit awaited us. It was the B1 cannon battery crew. They boarded the bus as well and we continued towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, how many men did you take with you all together, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Around 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at what time did you arrive at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Around 1.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, had you been to the Zvornik Brigade before?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what happened when you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade? Can you describe exactly what happened when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We arrived in front of the command building of the Zvornik Brigade. We parked the bus. I got off and went to the military police reception office where there were two MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you introduce yourself, or what did you do with these MPs?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I introduced myself and that I was to report to the Zvornik Brigade command. At that point one of the MPs picked up the phone. Having completed that conversation, he told me that we were to go together to see the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, at this point I would like to show you a picture. If I can have in e-court, please, 3D501. I would ask you, sir, to look at the picture that will appear in front of you, and to tell me if you recognise what is in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is the former command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, the perimeter of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see on this picture the place where you went in where you met those two military policemen?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see the reception office on the right-hand side. I believe that a lady's figure is depicted there in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I will now ask the court usher to provide you with a pen so that you can mark this picture. This is a special kind of pen, sir, that allows you to make markings on the screen in front of you. What I would like you to do is to write the number 1 where you went in to see those two military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you sign at the bottom of this picture, and write the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing this picture anymore. If we can save it in e-court, please. Sir, before I showed you this picture, you said that one of the military policemen told you that we were to go together to see the duty officer. Describe to us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When the MP told me that he was to escort me, we went together to see the duty officer at the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So where did he take you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He took me to the first floor in the building to the right from the reception office, and he took me to the first office on the right-hand side where the office of the duty officer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who did you meet there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As I entered the room, I found duty officer or his deputy there, and it is only logical that it was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why would that be, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. It's not clear. He needs to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you heard the comment from the Presiding Judge. The question is, was it the duty officer or the deputy duty officer, and how did you figure that out, if you did?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It would be logical that the assistant duty officer is on duty after midnight, and before midnight it would be the duty officer. That is a rule that was applied everywhere in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did the person you meet who was on duty introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, it's still not clear. The previous question which I found unclear was, "And who did you meet there," and he answered, "As I entered the room I found duty officer or his deputy there, and it's only logical that it was his deputy." Now, having heard him reply to your second question, it's important that one ties it up to the time frame when he went into this office. But then, if you read his answer, at least as we have it in the transcript, it would mean that it would have been the duty officer -- he says it is would be logical that the assistant duty officer is on duty after midnight and before midnight it would be the duty officer. So this time it was before midnight, I take it, not after midnight. It was after midnight?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will clarify, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it was after midnight then it would be the duty officer and not his deputy. This is how one reads his answer to your second question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you for your comments, Mr. President, and I'll clarify this, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you just clarify if with the witness. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in that room where you went in, how many persons were there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There was just one officer or commissioned officer in that room. I did not see him wearing any insignia on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you confirm whether it was the duty officer or the deputy duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This was the room where duty officer was on duty until 2400 hours, and after 2400 hours until the following morning, it was the assistant duty officer who would be on duty in that same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. But did you establish who was there? Do you know for a fact if it was the duty officer or the assistant duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can only assume that it was the deputy, judging by my previous experience, but I can't be sure of that because the person did not introduce himself to me as either the duty officer or his assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did that person give you his name?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I suppose he did, but as you will understand, none of us will really retain the name of the person when we first hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did he military policeman who was with you, what did he do at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The MP returned immediately. I suppose that he went back to his duty post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you tell the person on duty?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I introduced myself, and I told him that I had arrived on the order of Colonel Blagojevic and that I was supposed to report to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was his answer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He told me that Major Obrenovic was asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how did you react to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I told him that I was supposed to report to the brigade commander and that he should be informed of my arrival because I had arrived on the order of my superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He left the office and did not return for the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when he returned, sir, did he tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He said that I should take my unit into the compound and to billet them in one of the rooms and to be at ready until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you know at that time who was acting as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I knew it at the time because Colonel Blagojevic had told me that it would be Obrenovic down there when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you know personally Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you know which position he held?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I know that he was their Chief of Staff on the eve of Operation Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did your commander tell you any reason why he sent you to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He told me that we were to expect a major onslaught of the Muslim forces from Tuzla and that we were supposed to go there and assist the units in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, my question was not clear. You said two things in your testimony that I would like to clarify. You said that you had been -- that you wanted to see the commander of the brigade, but you said that Colonel Blagojevic sent you to see Obrenovic who you know to be the Chief of Staff. How do you reconcile the two?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I suppose you did not understand me well. I said that I'm supposed to report to the brigade commander because it is only logical that if my officer had ordered me to report to the brigade commander, that's who I was supposed to report to. However, at the time I was aware of the operation in Srebrenica and I was aware of the fact that the commander was engaged in Srebrenica and I also knew that Obrenovic by establishment was acting as the brigade commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you know Dragan Obrenovic personally, I mean, what he looked like physically?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He was somewhat taller than me and he was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you have recognised him if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he had been a good commander in the Posavina theatre in Croatia and I knew him from several situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, based on the information you obtained that night, where did you think that Obrenovic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I could conclude from various pieces of information that Obrenovic was in his office, probably resting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you find it unusual that he did not get up to greet you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not find it unusual. It was his free estimate when he could rest, as far as I could see it. And if the situation had been different, if we had to be engaged immediately, I'm sure that he would have gotten up and he would have issued orders himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what did you do after this encounter with the person on duty?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The gentleman told me to go back to the reception office, to take my men and to take them to certain buildings and to give them some time to rest, but also to be prepared for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So tell us where you went at that time and exactly what you did.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I returned towards the reception office where I was awaited by the same MP who took me to the duty officer. He made it possible for the bus to enter the compound, and when the bus entered the compound, I ordered my soldiers to take their personal gear and weapons and together we headed for one of the rooms after the same MP who was leading us there. We were billeted in a room that looked like a storage with a big door. This is where we stayed until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, in your last answer you say that the military policeman made it possible for the bus to enter the compound. How did he do this?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As I was walking towards the MP, I'm sure that the duty officer had called the MP and ordered him to lift the barrier for the bus to enter the compound, and I'm sure also that he had told him where to billet us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, once the bus entered the compound, where did it go inside the compound for your men to exit the bus?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We entered through the main gate, past the reception office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how far inside the compound did you go before your men exited the bus?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'll try to clarify. Once the bus goes in the barracks, where did it go inside the barracks before the men got off the bus?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There's so much room in front of the reception space that a bus can turn around without much manoeuvring.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it's my turn not to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it important?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I think so, Mr. President. I think that we need to know where the men left the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. If it is important, proceed. Otherwise, let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did the bus drive far inside before the men left the bus? That's all I want to know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When the bus entered the compound and when it was in, it stopped and we exited. I'm talking about 10 to 15 metres, the length of the bus. And as soon as we got off, we continued walking towards the room where we would be billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What did you tell your men as they exited the bus, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I told them that we would be taken to a room where we would rest, that we should remain at ready and that we would be probably be engaged if the situation so required.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And once the bus was empty, where did it go?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The bus went back to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what did your men do during that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Most slept in the room, and some left the room and remained outside. They were talking, smoking, chatting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you personally, what did you do during that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was sitting in front of the room where the rest of my troops were resting. I was with the group that was chatting and smoking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you sleep at all that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you see any vehicles coming in or out of the brigade during the night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you see any other buses anywhere else in the barracks compound that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you see any prisoners that night?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And during the time you spent at the Zvornik Brigade, did you meet with anyone else, and if so, when and who?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the morning around half past 8.00, a group of my soldiers together with me went towards the reception room. I encountered a soldier who wore military overall. He was well groomed, nicely dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did this man tell you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That soldier told me to give him my men to accompany him on a mission of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you accept?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And why not? And how did this take place?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I answered him that he couldn't have my soldiers because I was responsible for them and I did not have the approval of the commander to lend my troops to anybody else. We engaged in a somewhat serious exchange of arguments which could have turned into an incident at any moment. And at one point Drago Nikolic appeared on the left-hand side. I believe that he was the security officer in that Zvornik Brigade. And Dusko Nikolic was also with him. He was a military policeman in the Zvornik Brigade. He was a colleague of mine, the latter was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did they take part in that discussion you had with this man?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, both sided up with me. Dule was very harsh and gave the man a piece of his mind, so the man realised that he had made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what did this man do following this heated discussion that you described?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he went next. Dule, Drago, and I remained there. We actually turned towards the reception room, and there we talked, we reminisced on our experiences and Dule took out a pistol, 7.62 that had he confiscated on a mountain from the Muslim army. We had a few laughs, we talked about our former experiences because the three of us went to elementary school together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, this young man and well groomed that you met and that you had this discussion with, do you know who he was, or did you know at the time who he was, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you later confirm who he was?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I only assumed that this was the notorious Lukic but I can't be sure of that because nobody referred to him by his name or address him, so I can only suppose that that was the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was this man wearing a rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. I have already told you that he wore an overall without any insignia on it. I couldn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Drago Nikolic or Dusa Nikolic tell you who he was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Had they known, I'm sure that they would have told me or at least they would have addressed him by his name, or at least Dule would have while he had the heated exchange with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, did it appear to you that Dusa Nikolic or Drago Nikolic in fact issued an order to this man?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what time was it, sir, when all this happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I believe that it could have been any time between half past 8.00 and 9.00 or maybe to be even more precise, it was around 20 to 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, you mentioned that Dusan Nikolic was a schoolmate of yours. What else did you know about Dusan Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I knew everything. We went to school in Kravica together, together with Dragan Nikolic, we completed elementary education together. Dule then enrolled in the construction school then went to reside in Sarajevo. There he married, he had a wife and two children. As the operations started in 1992 he returned to his home town, actually to Zvornik, and that's how he joined the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: How about Drago Nikolic, how much did you know Drago Nikolic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We knew each other because we went to elementary school together for eight years. After that Drago completed the military secondary school in Sarajevo. There he remained working, and we would often see each other at gatherings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you notice that morning how Drago Nikolic was dressed?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: During when you saw him that morning.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was well dressed, nicely groomed, clean shaved. He always made sure that he was nicely dressed and well groomed and that was the case that morning as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, was your unit given an assignment at the Zvornik Brigade that morning?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We did not receive any assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what did you do, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Around 10.30 I was by the gate. Major Dragan Eskic appeared. He was the personnel officer at the Bratunac Brigade. He was followed by Zoran Kovacevic. Major Eskic approached and said that Colonel Blagojevic sent replacements. I welcomed that news and I accepted the replacements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what did you do -- what did you and your troops do at that time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I returned immediately to the room where some of the soldiers were. I ordered that they pick up their weapons and equipment and start boarding the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where did you go with the bus?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Once on the bus we went towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, before leaving with your men to Bratunac, did you speak to Obrenovic before leaving?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you return to see the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There was no need. Since the replacements came, I believe that the person in charge of them was supposed to go to see him and receive his orders, and I was supposed to return to my brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, if that morning you had received a tasking from the Zvornik Brigade, what would you have expected to happen? How would this have taken place?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Had there been any need for us in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, I would have been summoned to the brigade command. There the commander would be supposed to issue oral orders and assignments, and then I would have to be taken to the area of responsibility of the unit that I was supposed to assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what kind of information would you expect to have received in such a briefing, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I would certainly be seen by the brigade commander. He would issue the tasks and orders personally. He would tell me what we were supposed to do in that direction, and from what direction we could expect the enemy to appear. He would also probably choose an officer who would escort me to the area of responsibility of any of the battalions of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, sir, going back to just the time before you left, did you speak with those two men who came from the Bratunac Brigade? I'm talking about the two men you spoke with, I think you mentioned the names Eskic and Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We spoke briefly, as I said. I talked to Major Eskic who told me that he brought another unit that was supposed to replace my unit on Colonel Blagojevic's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you see how many men were with them?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What time did you arrive in Bratunac on that day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think around 12.00 or 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what happened once you returned to Bratunac? Were you given another assignment?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I returned to the Bratunac Brigade command, I dismissed my troops. They went home. I reported to the brigade command and I found Colonel Blagojevic there. We greeted each other and I can say that we were both happy. He was happy because I had gone to fulfill the task, and I was happy because he made good on his promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, what was your next military assignment given to you by your commander, and when was that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, it was Monday, my commander set out towards Zepa. He told me that I should remain in the AOR of the brigade, and that I should go to the area of Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what were you supposed to do in the area of Sandici?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the area, there was a task I had to carry out. The 3rd Infantry Battalion Commander Zekic and the Workers Battalion had been ordered to go to the area to search the terrain between Sandici, Kamenica, Krajinovici and Mratinci towards Konjevic Polje to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What were you searching the terrain for?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We had to search the terrain because some units were along the road securing the road for regular traffic. Therefore, we had to search the rest of the terrain for any enemy soldiers left behind so that they would be removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you have any information that soldiers, enemy soldiers were left in that area?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There certainly was some information to that regard because we would not have been ordered to search the terrain otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, at what time did you set out to perform this task?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Between 12.00 and 12.30. I had been given a task to link Jevic who was the head of the MPs, and Zekic who was in charge of the 3rd Battalion the area, I was supposed to serve as a link between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, just to be sure, you say between 12.00 and 12.30, is that around noon?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you recall, how many men participated in this search?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In total around 300 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how long were you busy completing this task?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: One afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall who was in overall command of this search?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The operation, as I said, included Zekic who was commander of the 3rd Battalion. He was responsible for his unit. Jevic was responsible for the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And who were you responsible for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Just to clarify the record, there was a reference on my LiveNote at page 26, it's gone now, probably about line 10 or so to Jevic being in charge of the military police and just so we have it clear on the record that may have been what he said but I'm confident my friends from the Borovcanin team would like this clarified as well, if that's indeed what he said or he said something else so there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's correct in the transcript where you refer to page 26, line 10 because what you are referring to page 25, lines 20 and 21 presumably. That's where we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- "I had been given a task to link Jevic who was the head of the MPs, and Zekic who was in charge of the 3rd," whatever it is, the area. So, Mr. Bourgon, will you look into that, please, and clarify with the witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand, and can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an error interpretation. Dusko Jevic was in charge of the police. Not the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer, and thank you, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on, sir, while you were performing this search, what was your role? That was my next question before my colleague stood up. What was your role in that search?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My role was to serve as a link between Dusko Jevic, that is the police force, and our battalion and its commander Zekic. They were supposed to meet up, whereas the left flank of our battalion was next to a battalion of the military brigade, probably, because we were doing the search simultaneously. This is the area that I hale from in Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall seeing anything unusual while this search was conducted?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber exactly what you saw?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As we were deploying our units from Sandici and the asphalt road there to the south, we set off for Bratinci. It was the start point of the search. When we arrived in the area of Kamenica, we noticed a large group of corpses. The site was horrific. It smelled awfully. There were so many of them that you could move from one corpse to another without ever touching the ground, there were that many dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, who were those dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: A great many of them was -- were in military uniform. I suppose they were members of the 28th Division. Some of them wore civilian clothes, as it was their custom to change into civilian clothes frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did you see any dead bodies of women or children?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not see any children or women.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know how these people died?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the spot, you can see everything. Many of them had killed themselves by activating hand grenades. Some of them killed themselves with their weapons. Some of them took out their belts and hanged themselves from the trees. It was gruesome to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You say there were so many of them. Can you give us an estimate of how many bodies were lying there in the field that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It is in the part that I covered, I saw several hundred dead people, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, were there any ambush operations conducted in that area by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know precisely what the answer would be, but judging by the stories I heard later, I arrived at a different conclusion that I can share with you later, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What I'd like to know from you is, you said that some people killed themselves by activating hand grenades and some killed themselves. Did they all kill themselves or were there other reasons for them, for these bodies to be lying there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There must have been clashes inside the group as well. According to the information we have, some of them had wanted to surrender, whereas the others had not. You could see that some were shot from firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that. Sir, when you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, just a second. Mr. Gavric, what you saw at the time was just dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How could you know that they killed themselves by activating grenades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you see a person lying on the ground with his or her lower part of the lower body completely blown off or up then it means that that person put a hand grenade underneath and activated it. On the other hand, if you see somebody with a bullet hole in their skull, in the temporal area, that indicates that it was a suicide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They would have been killed by the hand grenade that was thrown by the enemy or the opponent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would have been really super to get 20 metres away from a group which counted 15 to 20.000 and to throw a hand grenade in such a situation. But you could see the dead bodies and you could see the ground they had covered, not a single blade of grass had remained there, and you could clearly see the area that they were moving through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, moving on, did you capture some prisoners during this search?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you describe -- do you remember approximately how many prisoners you captured?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Precisely 38 people. Three of whom were under-age children.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you do with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Dusko Jevic took the prisoners to the area of Konjevic Polje. As for the three minors, I put them in my vehicle and took them to the Bratunac Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So beginning with the prisoners that you gave to Dusko Jevic, to your knowledge what happened to these prisoners after?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know. The next day I had to go to Sokolac on private business and I went through Konjevic Polje. In front of a former store, I saw a group of people picking up paper and litter in front of those buildings that were there, and I recognised them as the prisoners of the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And moving on to the three minors that you referred to do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Upon arrival in Bratunac, I took the three children to the military police premises. I ordered them to give food to the children, to bathe them, and to treat them properly. It was rather difficult because the children would not be left behind and they were holding on to my pants. I suppose that while we were in the field, they felt protected by me. It was a difficult situation and it would be too much for me to tell you all the details of what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if those three minors are still alive today?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I handed them over and they were exchanged for nine policemen who had been captured near Zvornik. I think they haled from Doboj. In 2001 or 2002, I saw them in Tuzla. I had wanted to meet some of those children there and it was made possible for me to do by Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did Naser Oric ever tell you who these three minors were?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When we met at the Tuzla hotel and had lunch, we discussed the topic. He laughed and he said, the two boys, the twins told you they were from Karacici. They did not want to tell you that they were my cousins, because they were afraid of being killed. And I told him well, who would be such a person to be able to kill a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just one last question before I move to my next topic. I'd just like to come back to those bodies that you saw, those hundreds of bodies. You mentioned that many committed suicides and you were asked questions by Judge Kwon concerning the grenades. But do you know really how they died, all of these people, or you just notice how some of them died?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I'll explain. When the children surrendered they got on to the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. They were playing, saying that it was nice to move along a road which was not mined. I asked them many a question about how they survived, had they survived the trip and they told me everything. They said that they ate wild pears, that someone killed a sow, that is how they survived. They also told us of the suicides or people killing each other. They said that at certain points some would get depressed and such a person would simply take out his rifle and spent all of his ammunition before being killed, spraying bullets and killing everyone near. They also had some bombs which I never saw, and they were explaining that as well. They also said that many people stepped on landmines. That is what they were telling us. They also said that they were fired at by artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I now move to a different topic which is the days preceding the fall of Srebrenica. And my first question is how close is Bratunac to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, what was the involvement of the Bratunac Brigade in the events leading to the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995? What was the task given to the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The main task of the Bratunac Brigade was to defend the town of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did any component of the Bratunac Brigade take part in the combat operations on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which one, if any?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The red beret platoon. I know that they were along the axis including checkpoint 789.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: 879.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember what was the code name for the fighting that was directed toward Srebrenica in mid-July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I believe it was called Krivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, at that specific moment were you the chief of artillery of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And within a brigade such as the Bratunac Brigade, to whom does the chief of artillery report?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The chief of artillery is a staff officer responsible to the brigade commander. In my case, that would be Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you share with us, what is the role and the duties of the chief of artillery in the brigade? What is it that did you at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The main task of the artillery chief is to assist in the preparation of orders in the field of artillery to the brigade commander. All the other chiefs do the same concerning their types of weaponry. Such a person also needs to control the firing and targeting if in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, who exercises command over the artillery resources of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The artillery officers are commanded by the chief of artillery, who in turn is commanded by the brigade commander. Some of the artillery officers also include officers of the different batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, when we hear that the artillery supports the battalions, what is the role of the chief of artillery in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Battalion commanders in this case could require artillery support from the chief of artillery, and in this case it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So just for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, what do we mean by requesting support from the chief of artillery? In practical terms what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If one of the units on their axis faced an enemy attack or noticed enemy movements, then the commander of that unit, or in this case, the commander of that battalion, could request for me to provide him with artillery support on the wing where such movements were noticed or where such an attack was encountered, and this type of fire is known as preventive fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. One last question, Mr. President, maybe we can go for the break is, what were exactly the artillery resources or assets of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade had a mixed artillery group consisting of a battery of cannons B17, 60 millimetres consisting of five tools, two 105 howitzers and 1 to 2-millimetre cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I think we can stop for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since Judge Agius has to attend an official meeting this afternoon, so we'll be herein carry on sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when we left off before the break, you told us what were the resources in terms of artillery which the Bratunac Brigade had.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question has to do with the fighting which was led towards Srebrenica. When did you initially receive orders to take part in the events leading to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And how did you receive your orders on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It was a written order by the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what was the task given to the artillery of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The task given to the artillery group was to defend the town of Bratunac together with the units of the 1st and the 2nd Infantry battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And where were the guns of the Bratunac Brigade located?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The brigade artillery group took up three firing position. One was by B1 cannons, northwest of the town of Bratunac in the sector of Repovac village. The howitzer platoon 105 millimetres was by the brickworks, in the brickworks sector which was north, northwest 1.500 metres from the town. The 1 to 2 millimetre cannon platoon was north of the town 2 kilometres away from the town in the Ravne sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when the guns of the Bratunac Brigade were firing, where were you physically?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My position was at the artillery observation point, the checkpoint 438 at the advance positions of the Defence of the town at the artillery observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, who selected the place where the artillery observation post would be, and what factors do you use when you choose this location?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In keeping with the rules of service, the chief of artillery is the one who selects and proposes to the commander the observation post of the artillery, and the commander either accepts that or not under what conditions. Several criteria are used. The observation post should be a dominant position as close as possible to the forward defence line in order to be able to observe the artillery fire and forward defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So when the guns are firing, the chief of artillery, is he located with the guns or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. The chief of artillery was at the Koalin hill observation post at checkpoint 438, and the firing positions were some 3 to 5 kilometres backwards from the forward firing -- defence positions which is according to the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the chief of artillery must relay the orders of the brigade commander to fire, how do you communicate with the guns?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You communicate by wire connection, this is the best way if at all possible, and we did have those conditions, and we also used radio communication as required so we used both types of connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again just to clear up the record, there's a reference to the observation post hill, which I presume we'll be referring to on more than one occasion. And I think the witness stated that, but we probably should have it spelled correctly in the record since it tends to get misspelled in other places as well. So if we could have that clarification for the hill at checkpoint 438, I'm sure the witness can spell it for us, if we could have that clarification, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take up the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand exactly what my colleague is looking for but I think that the witness can confirm where the artillery observation post of the Bratunac Brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Page 36, line 4 on my LiveNote. I think we can all agree what it is, I'm happy to put it on the record, but I'd just as soon hear it from the witness and spell it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So where is that location, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This was elevation 438, midway between the left wing of the 1st Bratunac Battalion and the second wing of the -- and the right wing of the Bratunac Brigade defence and it was the forward defence line of the town, so you end up with a triangle with the observation post in its centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe he referred to a particular hill name, begins with a K.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kaolin hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kaolin Hill, K-a-o-l-i-n, hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, to the best of your recollection when exactly did Srebrenica fall, on what day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of December [sic] 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is there an interpretation mistake, I'm not sure. Did you say December?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I apologise, 11th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, during the period when you initially received your orders, that is 6 July as you mentioned earlier, and the 10th of July 1995, were the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fired?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The 122 millimetres M31/37 opened fire on the village of Studenac on the north slopes of Gradac hill. This is the place which was once inhabited by Serbs and which was then torched, and it was some 3 kilometres in front of the observation post as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did this take place -- on which day did this take place? I was referring to the period from the 6th to the 10th of July, so on which day did this take place?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This took place on the 11th of December [sic]. I apologise, 11th of July. I do it every time, I mixed up my months and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So I'll say my question over again. From the 6th to the 10th of July, which of the guns the Bratunac Brigade fired, if any?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Between the 6th and the 10th of July, including the 10th of July, we did not open artillery fire. I said that it only happened on the 11th. I may have misunderstood your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 11th of July, you mentioned that there was the 122-millimetre gun which opened fire on the village of Studenac. Now, did any other guns of the Bratunac fire on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At that moment, no. But after that the 105-millimetre howitzers did open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you also mentioned that this -- when there was firing, you mentioned that you fired on that village, which was once inhabited by Serbs. Why would you fire on this village?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Six months prior to the operation we had moved the firing positions of our 122-millimetre cannons. The battery commander had to correct his aim and it just so happened that I thought that they had failed to do that, and I had reports from the field that our units had been advancing towards Srebrenica, and I expected at any moment the Muslim forces could engage in a counterattack. And in order to be absolutely sure about the aim of these tools, I ordered the elements to be checked and it turned out eventually that I had been right all the time about the aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, on the record, we get the word "tools," about the aim of these tools. Are you referring to the aim of the guns?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Guns, the artillery pieces. Whenever you need to change your firing position, you have to rectify and coordinate your aim according to the rules of artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is that the type of fire that you did on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the type of fire which had been ordered. I was not happy with the aim and that's why I ordered the pieces to be checked, and once the fire was corrected and as soon as that was done, we were able to hit our imaginary target in the village of Studenac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt my colleague, but I found that some words of the witness's are not translated despite he told it three times. He used the B/C/S word "nisanske sprave," and it was translated as "aim".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The correct translation of which should be what, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is aiming equipment or aiming tool or something like that. Not aim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your observation is noted and will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is a part of artillery piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll bear that in mind in hearing the evidence or reading the transcript later on. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you my colleague for his observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall when the population of Srebrenica left to go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of July around 1200 hours I received a report from the elevation 73, also known as Caus about a large group of the population gathering in the vicinity of the gas station in Srebrenica below the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fire on the population as it was moving towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fire close to these people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer. Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Could you say your answer over again?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If you were asking me whether the guns opened fire close to these people, my answer was no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What is the closest to these people that the guns of the Bratunac Brigade were fired, if at all?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Fire was not open anywhere close to them, but sometime later, and I can tell you about that, it was 2 to 2.5 kilometre east from the route along the which the population moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, if it had been the intention of the Bratunac Brigade to fire the guns at the civilian population, technically was this possible?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What would have been the result if the Bratunac Brigade had intended to fire its guns at the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It would have been a massacre. It was a large group of people, between 40.000 and 50.000 people moved along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, to your knowledge did the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fire in or around the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari where the civilians were?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fire on the enemy at any time on 11 July onwards?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Around 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Where did the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fire, and why?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We noticed below elevation 877, the so-called Divljakinje [phoen], some of the Muslim forces that were engaged in defence and that's when we opened fire on those enemy units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, at this point I'd like to show you a document. If I could have in e-court, please, 5D1107. Sir, a document will appear on the screen before you. Looking at the first page I would like to know if you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It is an order by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is this the order that you were referring to concerning what happened in Srebrenica later on?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I will go through these pages on the screen in front of you. I would like to know if you can see in these documents the tasks that were issued to you or that were issued to the artillery of the Bratunac Brigade. If we can have the second page on the screen. If I can now go to the third page. And finally on the fourth page. I'll show you also the next page, I thought that was the last one, but if we can go to page 5 also. Sir, looking at this document, have you seen so far the tasks issued to the artillery of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I believe that on the page that I have in front of me, there's no bullet point 6. It should be bullet point 6 specifying those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can go one page back on this document towards the end. So what is this paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the tasks of the brigade artillery group of the Bratunac Brigade of howitzers and other artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can move to the next page at the top. So we see that paragraph 6 is continuing at the top of the other page, is this also related to the tasks issued to the artillery of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This was Lancer [phoen] 128 millimetre and these were also tasks of the Bratunac Brigade. If you are referring to bullet point 6.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, sir, I'd like to draw your attention to 6.2 where it says, and I will read that in English: "At 0300 hours on 6 July 1995," I'm not sure if it's a correct translation but it says, "it will fire four projectiles (50 kilogram air bombs) on the Potocari sector, (the school the 11th March factory, the Gracic hill at elevation 377, and Kula and Orici). My question is, did the Bratunac Brigade fire these four projectiles?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So why does it appear in this order and it was not done by the Bratunac artillery?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This was just an idea, a plan, but this doesn't mean that everything that is planned has to be implemented in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like now to show you a new document. If I can have in e-court please, P3358 [Realtime transcript read in error "P3588"]. I would like you to take a look at this document that will appear on the screen before you and to tell me if you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Who drafted this document, and what is it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I drafted the document and I sent it to the command of the Drina Corps, and in the document you can see why I sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, according to this document, it says that fire was opened on Srebrenica at 1907 hours. Was that the reason for sending the document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, this document was not sent because of that. The reason was the fact that our artillery piece broke down, we had to inform the command who were supposed to send us a repairman to try and deal with the problem on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another document. If I can have in e-court now document P3359. Sir, I'll show you a second document. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is this document related to the first one or the one that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
