utterances.text: Sir, once again here it says in paragraph one that the guns of the Bratunac Brigade fired on Srebrenica. Do you recall why the guns fired on Srebrenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On that day from the area of Budak fire was opened on our firing positions. We also noticed an enemy tank that had opened the fire. Then we received an order to destroy that tank. We used anti-tank -- anti-armour ammunition which has a stronger recoil than other ammunition, and as we were doing that one of the howitzers got stuck and three of my men were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, it says here that the two shells fell or near the domavija feature. Do you know what is the domavija feature?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I know the facility. It is a former hotel which I believe housed the command of the 28th Division or one of their battalions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Colonel Lazic is?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I know Colonel Lazic only as a person who was from the Drina Corps command. He was on duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, did this Colonel have the authority to order you to fire the guns of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He arrived with an order, he had been ordered by someone from the corps that the artillery be used. That is for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a final document, sir. If I can have in e-court P2884, and I discussed this with my colleague previously, Mr. President, I would like to give the witness the paper version because this document is actually a map, and I would like to give him the paper version that was issued to us by the Prosecution. And in e-court, this is 2884. I only have a few questions and the witness just taking a glance at the document will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall I showed you this document during proofing?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sir, do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is engagement plan of the corps artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For what operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The Susica operation. That was the code name for the Srebrenica operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the plans that were prepared at the corps level or higher concerning operation Susica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was not familiar with it since it was on a higher level than that that I was at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the type of information included in such an artillery firing plan?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can interpret the plan. It was my job to do so, and I understand it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, we won't need this document anymore. Sir, if on such an artillery firing plan an UNPROFOR observation post was identified with a number, does that mean that you intended to fire the guns on the UNPROFOR observation post?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, and you can't find it in the Colonel Blagojevic's order either.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So why are certain locations identified on the artillery firing plan? Why do we identify locations on such a plan?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If there are favourable conditions that enable firing, we first must devise a plan of fire with all the features and locations represented that otherwise would be included on the map. Then distances are measured as well as angles needed to load the artillery pieces properly. The numbers and facilities marked may not be targets of such firing. They are simply there to enable the crew to react rapidly against the enemy and that we can quickly move from one object to another should the enemy move quickly. And also it is done to avoid any collateral damage that could result from us not having prepared the locations correctly when opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. How many times did you meet with me before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Twice in Bratunac and once in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did anyone from the Defence ask you to sign a statement before your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, sir, what kind of questions did I ask you when we met in Bratunac? What was I interested in?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You were interested in what my orders were to go to Zvornik, who met there. You also wanted to know about the number of victims in the area of Konjevic Polje in Sandici and what was the situation like during the operation in Srebrenica on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, did I or anyone from the Defence team of Drago Nikolic tried to influence your testimony in any way?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. You could have tried but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But what?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: There would be no effect. We would probably go our own separate ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just one minute, Mr. President. I want to check my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just one thing I forgot to ask you, sir, earlier on. We spoke about Dusan Nikolic. Do you know what happened to Dusan Nikolic in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, Dule Nikolic was killed in action. I received that information soon. I believe I was in town. A few days ago, I discussed those details with my brother who was the physician on duty in the Zvornik Brigade that day. He saw Drago Nikolic between 1.30 and 2.00 in front of the hospital. Drago told him that Dule had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Bourgon, if you could indicate the 65 ter number of the draft allegedly drafted by the witness, you said it's P3588, but I couldn't locate the document with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not sure I understand your question, Mr. President. The draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Actually not sent. The document we just now sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Oh, the first document which was drafted by the document [sic], the number I have is P3358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 3358, yes. The transcript said it's 3588. Okay. That's corrected. Would any of the Defence team cross-examine this witness? Yes, Mr. Borovcanin's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, we will have a brief cross-examination. I don't believe it will last more than 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for information, we'll break at 5.25 and we'll have a 20-minute break and we'll adjourn at quarter to 7.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to accomplish my task by that time. I mean by 5.25 of course. [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic. I'm Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin's attorney representing him before this Tribunal and I will have a few questions on his behalf. I also want to go through a number of documents with you. Should any of the questions I put to you be unclear to you, please tell me and I will reformulate it. I also wanted to warn you that you should pause between your answer and my question. Otherwise, there will be an overlap since we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony today you said that you participated in the search of terrain on the 17th of July 1995. You also said that during that operation together with the units of the Bratunac Brigade, there was a unit commanded by Dusko Jevic as well taking part in it. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was your starting point on the 17th of July, from where did you go to Sandici when the operation began?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We left in the front of the Bratunac Brigade command. I had two MP escorts and a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at that location?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It was at 12.15 exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that that morning when you set out there was a meeting in the Bratunac Brigade, to be more precise, at that meeting tasks were stipulated for the units which were to take part in the search?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting, but Commander Blagojevic briefed me and told me that some units from the military brigade and some of the units from Bratunac Brigade will take part, plus another MUP unit. Those were the units that were supposed to take part in the search operation in the area of Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But my question was this: You did not attend the very meeting?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the meeting was attending by Dusko Jevic as well and did he receive any tasks from the Bratunac Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that one day previously on the 16th of July 1995 in the evening there was another meeting between Dusko Jevic and Momir Nikolic in which Jevic was notified that his units were supposed to take part in the search?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As of the 15th when I arrived at the Bratunac Brigade command I was on leave until the 17th when Colonel Blagojevic answered his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore your answer is that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to do this again, but there's another passage at page 49, line 24. There's a reference to commander Blagojevic briefed me and told me that some units from the military brigade and some of the units from Bratunac Brigade will take part plus another MUP unit. I'm not sure again if that's a translation issue or what he said, but I think we can benefit from clarifying that before we go too further along. It just doesn't make sense the way it's sitting on the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Military brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can assist my colleague. I believe -- of course, I don't want to put words in witness's mouth, but he said literally Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Mr. Gavric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat. According to the oral orders I received at 12.00 from the Bratunac Brigade commander, I was supposed to go to the area of Sandici where my task would be to link up Dusko Jevic who headed the police force and our 3rd Battalion. On the left flank of our unit of the 3rd Battalion, there will be units from the Milici Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] thank you, Mr. Gavric. I believe this clarifies the misunderstanding. Today you were discussing Dusko Jevic's unit referring to it as a MUP unit. I wanted to clarify one thing. I read the transcript of your testimony in the Blagojevic case and I came across a piece of information you stated whereby you said that the entire unit was formed of deserters who fled Bosnia and left for Serbia. Can you verify that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Those were Serbian deserters collected all over Serbia. They were taken there and they were referred to as special police, but I wonder what sort of special police it was when these were all deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the search operation, you will agree, of course, that it usually follows after the end of combat and that the goal of such an operation is to locate and neutralise any remaining enemy soldiers, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I was talking about it, I said that it was our task in the field to search it so that it would be clear of enemy forces. And also, we were supposed to relieve the units which were securing the road between Konjevic Polje, Bratunac and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And of course, it's a fully legitimate military operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It is the ending part of an operation. In any country if there are terrorists in a given area, certain units are sent in to search the terrain, what else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Today you talked about a number of soldiers, members of the BiH army who surrendered and the children that you took away. Reading the Blagojevic transcript, I noticed something that I wanted to clarify with you. When you were on the road, as you said in the Blagojevic case, did you use a phone or some other means of communication to call Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I called from Pervane where the captured soldiers were. I reported to him and asked him what to do. He told me this: The people who surrendered should be handed over to Dusko Jevic so that he could take them to Konjevic Polje and they would be further transported to Bijeljina presumably, that was the order I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have a correction for the transcript. It is page 52, line 17. We were talking about Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, the chief of security of the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You received the order from Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: He was the person you informed about the existence of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I called the switchboard Momir Nikolic replied, I asked him what to do and he said, "You should hand them over to Dusko Jevic, you, however, are supposed to go back to Bratunac and we'll dispatch a bus."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now turn to some documents. The first one is 4DB00251. Could we please have it in e-court. It is 4DP00251. Mr. Gavric, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the upper left corner it says command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. The date is 14th of July 1995. It says search of terrain, order. Now that you have the document before you, to cut things short, I will only have a few questions for you, which I hope you can confirm. This is an order concerning a terrain search which is based on a Drina Corps command order dated the 13th of July 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In items 1, 2, 3 and 4 of this order, you can see the tasks for each of the infantry battalions of the Bratunac Brigade concerning the search, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of July 1995, the Bratunac Brigade had already ordered its battalions to search the terrain, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will -- I would like to move to another document. It is P121. Mr. Gavric, if I remember correctly, you have had occasion to see this document during the Blagojevic case testimony, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: The author of the document is Colonel Ignjat Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately he is deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What was Colonel Ignjat Milanovic's position in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat. What was the position, the function of Colonel Ignjat Milanovic in 1995, in July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think he commanded the Milici Brigade. I'm not certain though. I know that he was our Chief of Staff, then he left and I don't know what his subsequent position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can also see from the document that it was drafted on the 15th of July 1995 in Bratunac. Can you tell me who it was sent to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. The 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, this must have been sent to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Under proposal it says, "The command, the corps IKM, the Drina Corps command."

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, to the attention of the commander. It was Krstic who was the corps commander at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to ask you about. On the first page of the document, if you can see, we find that Colonel Milanovic was touring the lines on General Krstic's orders and that according to his information there were large enemy groups in the field east of the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje Road and that the Bratunac Brigade is searching the terrain and that it is about to break out to the lines mentioned here. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Please move to the next page. Around the middle of the page it says "proposal" and it is underlined.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what it says?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It says, "To authorize the commander of the 1st Bratunac Light Brigade, as commander of all forces participating in searching the terrain and that are engaged in blocking the enemy and carrying out the 'asanacija' of the field next to the road mentioned," and I don't see the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And in control?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, "And in control of the Kasaba-Drinjaca road because we have no one to appoint from the KDK. If you agree with the proposal --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that you read out the part that I find important.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. This proposal by Colonel Milanovic that was sent to the command of the Drina Corps for the commander of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Military Brigade be appointed the commander of the overall mission of the scouring of the terrain, was this proposal adopted?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was adopted, I only know about this order but I apologise, I remember that Stojanovic, Captain Stojanovic actually was appointed chief of staff in Milici, and Milanovic was transferred for -- to a new duty in the Drina Corps. I apologise. I've just remembered. You have jogged my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, let's move on to is different document which is P254. While we are waiting for the document it seems that we again have an omission in the transcript. You said that Ignjat Milanovic was transferred to the Drina Corps, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Nastic was the commander of the Milici Brigade and Stojanovic was the chief of staff. Now I know, you've jogged my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is a document which is a daily combat report dated 15 July 1995 sent by the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Under item one it says, "Strong enemy forces in front of the forward positions of the 4th Infantry Battalion on the brigade's right flank are carrying out combat activities and regrouping in the direction of Konjevic Polje and further on," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Further on we are reading under item 2 which reads, "Our forces are still searching the terrain in accordance with your strictly confidential order number 01/4-157/5 dated 13 July 1995." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It transpires from the document that the Bratunac Brigade on the 15th of July continues to search the terrain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it transpires from this document that the commander of the Bratunac Brigade carried out the order. If we are looking at the orders and the combat reports, this is what transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at another document, the number is P255. Mr. Gavric, this is something that you will agree with and confirm that this is a daily combat report sent on the 16th of July 1995 sent by the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade to the commander of the Drina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's now pay attention to the bottom part of the document. I'm going to read that part to you. I believe we will be able to go faster.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "The commander in the brigade in the course of the day carried out the inspection of all units which are blocking the enemy withdrawal," and it says in brackets, (the 1st Milici Light Infantry Brigade units of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment, parts of the MUP, and the 5th Engineering Battalion) defined their tasks and organised their joint action and communications." Can you confirm that this is indeed what it says in the document.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In other words, on the 16th of July 1995, the commander of the brigade was one who went into the field, issued orders and organised cooperation of all the units, at least this is what transpires from this combat report, wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And obviously all the units mentioned here are duty-bound to carry out the orders of the commander of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And let me just ask you this, what we have just seen now is actually in keeping with the proposal by Colonel Milanovic that we had an occasion to see awhile ago, and by which the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was proposed as the commander of the overall operation of the searching the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what Colonel Milanovic drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Gavric, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are more than welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any other Defence team? Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe this would be a good time for the next break and maybe I could start after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Point taken. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Gavric, my name is Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And I appear on behalf of General Gvero and on his behalf I'm going to ask you a few questions relative to your earlier testimony today. Since the two of us speak the same language I would kindly ask you to make a break before giving your answer to allow the interpreters to interpret our words correctly and to avoid any overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, in your testimony and in answering my learned friend Bourgon's questions, you said that from the 6th of July 1995 up to the 11th, as far as I understood you, in the evening were armed positions together with your unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. From the 6th to the 10th I was at the observation post and my units were between 3 and 5 kilometres behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, between the 6th and the 10th you were at the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, inclusive of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the observation post that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Our observation post was on Kaolin hill at elevation 438, and commands a view of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All that time between the 6th and the 11th you were at that observation post, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from that observation post you could observe the UN base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could see all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you could also observe Srebrenica, the area around the gas station and the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I could see the entrance into Srebrenica, the area around the football pitch, and the area east of the football pitch. I could also see the entrance into Srebrenica, and people at elevation 773 could also observe the gas station and some buildings close to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I could understand your answers provided to Mr. Bourgon, your unit throughout all that time did not have an order to open fire and they did not open fire on Srebrenica or the area around Potocari and I'm referring to the base.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: None of the units including mine had an order to open fire on the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As for the town of Srebrenica, we never opened fire on it and our firing positions did not allow us to target Srebrenica due to the very high surrounding hills. I'm talking about the town of Srebrenica here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From your observation post you could actually see if anybody else shelled the base and Srebrenica, you could observe the UN base in Srebrenica and the other observation post had a good view of the area around the gas station and hospital?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout all this time, did you ever receive a report from your observation post or did you personally see that the base was shelled or that the area around the base was shelled?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, I did not observe any shelling of either the base or the area surrounding the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You personally never issued an order or opened fire?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the base, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, before this Trial Chamber we heard a testimony and we also saw some reports about hundreds and thousands of shells that allegedly fell on Srebrenica and the environs of Srebrenica and the area around the UN base. Would that tally with the truth and would that confirm what you know?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that because I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have to clarify something, are you saying that you personally did not see or participate in the firing of hundreds and thousands of shells on Srebrenica and on the base during that period in between the 6th and the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In order to fire hundreds or even thousands of shells, you would need time. Nobody had that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later on, did you have an opportunity to observe the area after the end of the Operation Srebrenica, and did you enter Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't enter Srebrenica for the next six months. Many friends of mine did and I can share the information that I have with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the situation in Srebrenica, what did they found in Srebrenica, would that confirm the fact that hundreds and thousands of shells had been shelled -- fired?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: They say that there was a lot of fire wood, that there was some traces of shrapnel and infantry ammunition on the buildings. If so many shells had fell on -- fallen on Srebrenica, then you could not have entered it. It would have looked like Vukovar, it would have been completely destroyed and it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, before this Trial Chamber, we have seen reports sent by DutchBat to its command, and these reports allege that during those days when you were above the base in Potocari, dozens of shells fell around the base and that some even hit the base or the perimeter of the base, and that the hospital in Srebrenica and its environment also suffered from shelling by dozens of shells. What would you have to say to that, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsibility that no shells fell in the base or around the base in Potocari. As for the hospital this is the first time I hear it from you that hospital was hit by artillery ammunition. It was well sheltered, and I don't see how any artillery weapons could have targeted the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, if you could put a pause between the question and answer. So just wait a little bit more before you start answering. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the reports that you sent to your superior command you obviously submitted combat reports and you stated that there was no shelling and these reports had been sent upwards along the chain of command and you stated that you did not use any weapons against the UNPROFOR base and against civilians, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, my client, amongst other things, is charged with talking to UN representatives and provided them with false reports about the situation on the ground when he said that UNPROFOR members and civilians had not been targeted. This information was based on the combat reports that arrived from the field. His statements that I have just quoted, would they correspond to what you saw and what you know from the field, i.e., that there was no shelling of the UNPROFOR positions and that there was no attack on the civilian population or the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I repeat, in the area of Potocari where I was stationed, actually what I could see from the base, I can guarantee there was no such thing. As for Zeleni Jadar and djoko [phoen] brdo areas, if such things had happened then UNPROFOR soldiers would not have sought protection of our army from the Muslim forces because a soldier of DutchBat had been killed there as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, when my client claimed that UNPROFOR and the civilian population were not targeted by the units of the Army of Republika Srpska, he was telling the truth, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Of course. No normal person would have targeted a civilian population and there was no need and nobody did or could indeed order that UNPROFOR soldiers should be targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gavric, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa, do you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it's you, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone. Good evening, sir. My name is Nelson Thayer, I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good evening. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified in the Blagojevic case and I think you more or less affirmed it today that you were personally and directly subordinated to Colonel Blagojevic when you were serving as chief of artillery; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to spend a little bit of time going over the documents which you were shown concerning the shelling of Srebrenica in May, specifically 25 May 1995. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so you know, I'm going to spend sometime with you for the remainder of today and through tomorrow just proceeding as chronologically as I can. Just so you know how things are going to happen. I don't intend to jump around. I just want to kind of follow through your activities during this period of time. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the Blagojevic case, and this was at transcript page 8556, you testified that at that time your recollection was that from the 17th of April 1993 until the 11th of July 1995, the Bratunac Brigade did not fire at all in the direction of the enclave. You were then shown the two orders that we looked at earlier today, and you tried to explain as best as you could what you recalled being the reason for you firing those shells on the 25th of May. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I do, but those were not orders but combat reports sent to the command of the Drina Corps. That's the first thing. Second of all, it is true that in the Blagojevic case, I could not remember the period in May. I could only remember it when I saw the document and then I apologized both to the Trial Chamber and everybody else. I did not do it on purpose. I just omitted that. It just escaped my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I understand that I don't believe you had been shown those documents by any party prior to your testimony in Blagojevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I arrived here, I wasn't told that by Mr. Karnavas. It was on cross-examination on the part of the Prosecution that I saw that document, and it -- now it jogs my memory, but it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's look quickly at these two documents again. If we could have P03358, please. You see the document again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you correctly referred to this as a report, and it's an urgent report; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we can see at the bottom where it says submitted at 2010 hours. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I do, yes. 8 hours and 10 minutes p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And does this confirm then, that this was actually sent to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, it should have been sent to the corps. We were not the ones to send it. It was sent to the communications centre who was supposed to forward it to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your recollection of those days, did that howitzer ever get repaired, pursuant to your notification to the corps that you needed an urgent repair?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That howitzer was irreparable. That is to say, it was supposed to be sent back to the factory because the back section had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was that determination made based on the contact that you had with the corps, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, some people arrived and they stated that it had to be towed away for repair. It was taken away and was not returned until the end of the war. At least not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's put up P03359, please. If we could scroll up just a little bit on the B/C/S on the original, please. And here again, sir, can you see that this indicates that this was sent the 2110 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the Blagojevic case, let me just read to you your recollection at the time of why these shells were fired, and then I'm going to ask you some questions. At page 8558 you say: "It says that on the 25th I can guarantee now as to what was fired at in a certain locality. I'm trying together rewind the film in my mind, but this document isn't clear to me. It appears that I signed it. I know that there was back recoil and I had some people injured. Now, as far as I can remember, I can't believe that it was in 1995, although, yes, indeed it does say 1995, an enemy tank did fire at us from the front of the Muslim defence lines, from the first Muslim defence lines, and probably 99 percent certainty we probably did respond. Now, the anti-armour and anti-armour projectile was used to try to destroy the tank. Well, I suppose I wrote this, but I really don't remember that that was in 1995 at all. I really can't remember that." Then you were asked a follow-up question: "All right. Well, you wrote it and it's dated 1995, so I think it's safe to say that that is what happened in 1995; right?" And your answer was: "Judging by the date, yes, but judging by my recollections, no. I remember that people were injured and I remember that this back section became stuck and so on. When I think about it now and turn my mind back to those days, I remember that we were fired at from the Budak defence lines by an enemy tank on my fire positions because there was a group that had been filtered in, a group of their reconnaissance men. And when we saw this fire, we did target the tank, but I really don't remember that that was in 1995. And if it says we opened fire, then I suppose we did." Now, let me just ask you one question, have you had a chance to search your memory since 2004, has anything jogged your memory and has your memory changed at all since you gave those answers back in 2004 about this event?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: To tell you honestly, even today those details are not clear in my mind's eye. There were many things that happened and it is difficult for me to recall exactly. I know that three soldiers were injured, they were seriously injured, and that a part of the cartridge fell out, destroying completely the back section. I know that it was towed away for repair and I know we were informed from the observation post that we were being targeted from Budak. We tried to use that to target back. I guess either the piece was too old by that time or our charge was too strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, when you say Budak, that's sort of a general area. Can you tell the Trial Chamber based on your recollection where was that tank located? Can you give us some reference point as to where precisely as best as you can remember that tank was actually located at the time that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can go by the observers report. I was not observing that place since I was not in a position to do so. It is close to Potocari, close to the settlement of Potocari. It is a pine forest they used putting the tank in that area at the frontlines of Srebrenica defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you be more specific as to what location in your recollection actually received or was the target of the tank fire?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know how well I can explain the area. I can indicate it on the map. I don't know whether you are familiar with that area. If you knew it as well as I do, you would be able to understand easily. It is the forward line of defence where they had certain pieces dug in. They frequently used that part to have the tank or some artillery pieces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. But my question was, sir, what did the tank fire on? You said that you responded to tank fire. My question is, can you help the Trial Chamber, give a reference point, something to let them know where this tank was firing at or what received the fire? That's all I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think in the Blagojevic case, which should be in the transcript, that I said that our firing position was targeted. They missed and the shell fell at a distance from where our position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "our firing position," can you be more specific as to what that means? What firing position?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The firing position of our 105 howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, that was located where?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The firing position? It was located in the brickworks area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that this was something that had to be responded to quickly? You've got a tank, it's a mobile target, it has fired at your firing position and if you are trying to target it, as you said, you can't wait all day in order to fire at it. I see you are shaking your head. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When a tank is moving it can open fire, but it can also fire from a stationary position. The tank had been dug in and they were short of fuel. Therefore, the tank did not change position, at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, are you telling us then that it's essentially a sitting duck once it's fired, if it's dug in, it can't get itself out quickly?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In any case, if there was an embankment, and they probably had one, they would still need time to turn the engine on and leave it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you say you are targeting the tank, when you testified that you actually targeted the tank, do you recall whether you were successful in taking out either the tank or its position where it was dug in? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. All I know is that no more fire was opened at us from that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just had a chance to look at those two reports, your original report, and the interim combat from Colonel Blagojevic. Can you explain why the report clearly states that you targeted downtown Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know personally, but I think that in the report it is stated -- well, I know that we did not open fire at downtown Srebrenica. As for how many projectiles were fired from our position, well, I think it was four at the most. Once the cannon was no longer in operation and the people had been injured, we halted the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's take a look at P03559 again then, sir. You see the document in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 3359, Mr. President. Sorry if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, the report is clear and simple, sir, is it not, that in paragraph 1 it says: "Pursuant to Colonel Lazic's verbal order we fired two times two projectiles, in total four, if there was any question, from howitzer 105 millimetre on the Srebrenica town. Projectiles were fired at 1907 hours. Artillery observers from Pribicevac reported that two projectiles fell in the vicinity of the domavija building. The other two projectiles were not observed, but they definitely fell on Srebrenica." My question, sir, is you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President, my colleague is reading from the document or doing some editing the document as he reads along like "definitely fell on Srebrenica" and things like that. I don't see this on the document unless we don't have the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at the English translation that I've got here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably there may be some different versions of the English interpretation. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is the version that was shown to you, sir, during the Blagojevic trial. I'm looking at it right now. You've testified that tank was over near Potocari. I ask you again, it's clear that these shells were intended for Srebrenica town. Tell the Trial Chamber why in response to the tank fire from Potocari you target a hotel and Srebrenica town.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: First of all, from my firing positions no one could target the Domavija Hotel. It was in front of trig point 1113. No artillery piece, save for a mortar, could target that building from my direction. I seriously doubt the accuracy of that report. I would like to see a person who can hit domavija across that high -- over that high hill from the position where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So your explanation, sir, is this report has got it wrong; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I claim that we practically speaking could not hit that. It's simply not done. There is a factor, a group of angles that you have to calculate artillery use, and the end angle was simply not something we could achieve given that we had no mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier today that Colonel Lazic arrived with an order, and I just wants to clarify that with you. Is it your testimony that he arrived in person with an order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Colonel Lazic came personally to the brigade command. That is why I was trying to remember how that tallied with his arrival. It is certain that on that day when my report was drafted, there was a report sent to the brigade command, and I presume he arrived there personally conveying someone else's order from the corps command. Either that, or in the meantime, he was in contact with someone from the corps, but I had no insight in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And explain to us, please, why the Drina Corps operations chief needs to hand deliver an order to your brigade to permit you to open fire on a target that has been directly targeting your fire position?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can't explain that to you, who ordered and why. In terms of subordination, well, I don't know what his tasks were at the corps so that he would be able to say that he is going to order it. It's either that or he was there on some other business, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, is it your testimony, sir, as former chief of artillery, that you needed authorisation from the corps to fire on a target that had opened fire on your firing position in such a circumstance? You did not have the authorisation on your own to take that action? I just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, no. It was a protected area. Which one of us could do something that was prohibited, and for me, that was the law. I respected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is your testimony, sir, then to this Trial Chamber that the shells that you fired on 25 May 1995 were fired pursuant to an illegal order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If someone has the right to kill you without you responding, that's a different thing. In this case someone higher up probably decided that we can respond, having been provoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Tell us, sir, how much time elapsed between the tank firing on your firing position and Colonel Lazic's arrival to the Bratunac Brigade with this order that he is hand delivering?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I can't say. As I said, I recall it poorly. I remember the best that my men were injured on that occasion, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was it minutes, hours, can you help us at all?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Whatever I told you would not be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when Colonel Lazic hand delivered this order, sir, where did he take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait a minute, Mr. Gavric. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't like to interrupt my colleague but it's the third time that he suggests that there was a hand delivery of a document, but he put a question to the witness earlier on concerning whether the document -- there was in fact a hand delivered order --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we have the witness remove his earphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric. Mr. Gavric, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, but I understood the gentleman's question about Mr. Lazic's orders. I didn't see it and if they have one in writing, I'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could remove your headphone for the moment. I don't remember whose turn it is to speak, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President, I don't want to take too much time. On page 72 my colleague asked a question at lines 4 to 6 and he says, it is your testimony that he arrive in person with an order. And then the witness answered that there was no written order to his recollection. And the content of his answer is there. So I would just like that in future questions not to again come back and always suggest to the witness, again the written order, the written order, the carried written order. He had a response from the witness and then he can move on from there using the information that the witness provided to him. That's all I'm saying. I don't want to take too much time, but it would be more fair to the witness to at least put the right words that he himself answered. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's cross-examination but did he refer to written order, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Frankly, Your Honour, I thought he had. I thought he had testified about arriving at the Brigade with an order. Now, if that was just a verbal order, then fine, we can clarify that. My understanding or the implication I drew was that it was a written order, and in my questions to him he didn't correct me that it wasn't a written order, it was an oral order, so ... now, I'd be happy to try to clarify that with him and I certainly do intend to given what we have here in the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's do that and move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified earlier today about the first time that you disobeyed an order, and that you had sought a written order in connection with that order. You've just told us that firing on the Srebrenica town, the safe area, was something that you thought was in violation of the law, and that you needed higher authority in order to respond. It's your testimony, is it not, that you sought that authority from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: What authority?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The authority to respond by firing at the safe area.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I didn't seek it. There was a person from the Drina Corps there. It says it was Colonel Lazic. What I shared with you is my opinion, I did not receive a written document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that Colonel Lazic arrived with his order. What did he tell you about the order? And I understand now you are telling us it's an oral order; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You are asking me about something and I can only tell you this, my commander was there. I didn't talk with Colonel Lazic. It was Colonel Blagojevic that was in a position to talk to Colonel Lazic, not myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic was in command at this time, what was his position in May 1995, May 25th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It so happened that he was there on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what discussion did you have with Colonel Blagojevic about the need to secure authorisation from a higher command to fire on the safe area in violation of the law?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not discuss that with him. If a report arrived, the brigade commander was put in the picture and that's all that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just an intervention on the translation. Page 76, line 4, the witness did not say that Blagojevic was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, but that rather on that day he was given the duty and accepted the duty of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, you better ask the question again or --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- are you happy with the explanation of Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Absolutely. I understand what happened on the 25th of May, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why Colonel Lazic arrived. Now, I just realised when I rewound the whole film, he probably arrived to actually hand over the duties in the Bratunac Brigade on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So we all know that on this day Colonel Blagojevic assumed command of the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Now we know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't just find that out today, did you? Or did you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer questions that were never put to me. I was never asked when, on what day people assumed their duties, but I just realised that Colonel Blagojevic arrived on that day and assumed duties as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, so you can say that the cookie just crumbled, that the penny just dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's go back to what you told us a little while ago. Your recollection was that because you believed you were being called upon to break the law and fire on a safe area, you needed authorisation from your higher command. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I please ask the witness to remove his headset so that I can ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness never said what my colleague just repeated, that is, that the witness didn't want to do something that was not allowed by the law. What he said is that it was something that was not allowed, that such was the law, that it could have been prohibited by an order, by an order from the staff command, for example, so that accordingly he could not fire on the zone without an order from the high command. I think my colleague should first clarify this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll just read what the answer was to my question. My question was: "Now, is it your testimony, sir, as former chief of artillery that you needed authorization from the corps to fire on a target."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is page 72, line 21, Mr. President. I'll start over. "Now, is it your testimony, sir, as former chief of artillery that you needed authorization from the corps to fire on a target that had opened fire on your firing position in such a circumstance? You did not have the authorisation on your own to take that action? I just want to clarify that." And the witness's answer was: "No, no, it was a protected area, which one of us could do something that was prohibited, and for me that was the law. I respected it." I think it's quite clear what his response was, Mr. President, and that's why he explained that he was getting authorisation from a higher command. I'm simply following up on what this witness said quite unexpectedly, I would add, in the course of answering my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give me the reference again.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is page 73, line 1. Mr. President, with all due respect, for me it is not clear, was he prohibited by the law or by an order from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, all that needs to be said is that my witness [sic] is trying to put the words in the witness mouth that he was given and illegal order and the witness did not say that, Mr. President. The witness did not say that he received an illegal order. And I support the objection from my colleague representing Mr. Miletic, but also this has to be read in context what the witness said later on, and he said if someone has the right to kill you without your responding that's a different thing. In this case, someone higher up probably decided that we can respond because we had been provoked. That puts that into context and there was never any idea from the witness to say that he was issued an illegal order so that's what we just say my colleague simply should not put these words in the questions or ask him to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, it is our understanding that the witness said truly that it would be illegal to shell the protected area and said, he said it's the law, but we are not sure whether the order he received was such that he should target the protected area or so. If you could clarify with that, and then proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's what I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we do it in some efficient way. We have only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified that you believed that you were in no position to authorise firing into the safe area on your own; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that is because, as you said, you believed that that would be in violation of the law had you done that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I myself was not in a position to make such a decision. It was not my call.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you help the Trial Chamber by recalling what steps were taken within the brigade, within the Bratunac Brigade, to make that decision at a higher level? Who was involved, who had the discussions, and what were the discussions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I never attended those meetings. I never participated in that decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, tell us what you know about it, sir. We understand you might not have been there, but this was your firing position that had been fired upon. This was a decision that you've told the Chamber was something that you could not and did not want to make by yourself, so surely you must know what the discussions were even if you weren't there, who talked to whom in order to obtain authorisation to fire into the safe area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You read both reports, both Blagojevic and I say that Colonel Lazic was the man who was there, and that's the long and the short of it. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, can you explain that, please. You testified that Lazic was there, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I believe that on that day Colonel Lazic came on behalf of the command of the Drina Corps and carried out the changeover of the brigade commanders. What was said, where it was said, what discussions took place, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, did you ever receive an order either from Colonel Blagojevic or from Colonel Lazic to fire a shell on the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally don't remember whether I received an order to convey an order, whether it was ordered directly by Colonel Blagojevic or somebody else. I really can't remember. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we leave it at that and adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, we'll continue to hear your evidence tomorrow afternoon, so in the meantime, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Quarter past 2.00 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
